title: Sprint 7 (Godot) — Town and Conversation Systems

experience_slices.title: Start a game
experience_slices.description: Running the game opens a start screen in the Equinox look. A new game begins in the town the content names; loading a save picks up wherever it left off.

experience_slices.title: Walk a 3D town built from content
experience_slices.description: Whatever town the content describes — its walkable ground, buildings and obstacles, people, and spots — appears in 3D under the fixed-angle town camera with placeholder shapes, and the player walks it freely by clicking where to go.

experience_slices.title: People and spots in the town lead into conversations
experience_slices.description: Clicking a person walks the player into reach and starts whatever that person opens; spots open on interaction or when walked over, as the content sets. Walking pauses while a conversation runs and resumes when it ends.

experience_slices.title: Any written conversation plays on screen
experience_slices.description: One-on-one talks and narrated scenes with any number of speakers play as text and choices, and the player moves through them by choosing or continuing.

experience_slices.title: Choices shift who the player is; who they are opens options
experience_slices.description: Choices shift the player's personality, seen in their own readout rather than as numbers in the conversation, and some choices need a certain personality. A locked choice shows greyed with an in-world line, never its threshold (ADR-075), and every step has an ordinary fallback, so the player is never stuck.

experience_slices.title: People respond according to their archetype
experience_slices.description: Characters present react to the player's choices in keeping with their fixed archetype, so the same choice can land differently with different people and change how they feel about the player. Written reactions can replace or silence the default for a particular choice.

experience_slices.title: Earlier choices carry forward
experience_slices.description: Flags, remembered choices, and conversations already seen change later lines, choices, which conversations play, and the town itself — who stands where and what is open.

experience_slices.title: Choices shape the party; the player picks who fights
experience_slices.description: Conversations can win someone over or bring in a new recruit, and people can leave. One screen shows the player's personality, party, and fight lineup, and the player picks the lineup from the party. Every team-building direction still open is supported.

experience_slices.title: The town hands off to the fight
experience_slices.description: Content marks where the town ends; with a valid lineup the player leaves for the fight and lands on a clearly marked placeholder until Sprint 8 builds the fight.

experience_slices.title: Save and load from inside the game
experience_slices.description: The player saves to and loads from ten slots inside the game. A save keeps everything — the town and position, a conversation in progress, story memory, personality, party, lineup, relationships, and the hand-off — and stays playable after the content changes; saves from the foundation build still load.

experience_slices.title: Creative decisions go in as content
experience_slices.description: The designer hands over creative decisions in any form; Claude turns them into JSON content packs using a written guide. Characters, archetypes, towns, conversations, and fights all live in content, and the game checks content for dead ends and broken references before it plays. No code changes for a new story.

experience_slices.title: Stand-in content proves every mechanic
experience_slices.description: A clearly marked stand-in pack — a cast, a town, conversations and scenes — lets one playthrough touch all five mechanics and all three team-building directions and end at the hand-off. It is test material, not a creative draft.

tasks.title: Content packs
tasks.description: Game content comes from a content pack: JSON files plus a small pack index listing them. A pack becomes the game's read-only content — settings, characters, archetypes, synergy bonuses, and fights to start with; later tasks add starting party, towns, and conversations to the same pack. The Godot project plays from a pack on disk instead of content written in C#: the existing stand-in cast and encounter move into a pack, which T23 grows into the full stand-in pack. Tests can hand in their own pack.
acceptance_criteria: Settings, characters, archetypes, synergy bonuses, and fights described in a pack's JSON files become the game's content with no code change, and a new file is picked up by listing it in the pack index
A pack that can't be read, isn't valid JSON, or doesn't fit the content format is refused with the file and place of each problem, never a crash
The Godot project and the smoke run play from a content pack on disk rather than content written in C#, and tests can hand in their own pack
Loading godot/content/standin through a FolderContentSource produces content equal to what StandInContent.Create produced before it was deleted
A pack with problems in several files reports a problem from each file in one load, each with its file name and JSON location (pointer, or line and column for syntax errors)
GameHost with a failing pack exposes the problem list and no session, and does not throw; changing the ancient_order/content/pack project setting changes which pack loads
tasks.technical_approach: Lives in the rules library under rules/AncientOrder.Rules/Content/Packs/ (namespace AncientOrder.Rules.Content.Packs), in three layers that mirror the save format (ADR-068). (1) Format records: sealed records that describe the JSON files exactly and are never the rules records. PackIndexFile { format: "ancient-order-content", version: 1, id, name, standIn: bool, files: [relative paths] }. ContentFile has optional sections: settings (object), synergy (object), characters, archetypes, fights (arrays); later tasks add towns and conversations to ContentFile and new fields to these records. They are read with a System.Text.Json source-generated context (ContentJsonContext) in strict mode: camelCase names, UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow, RespectNullableAnnotations, RespectRequiredConstructorParameters, no duplicate properties, AllowTrailingCommas, comments skipped. Enums are read only as exact camelCase names through a strict converter (generalize SaveEnumConverter into Common). Polymorphic records (conditions and effects from T2-T9) use [JsonPolymorphic(TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName = "type")] with AllowOutOfOrderMetadataProperties = true, so authors write { "type": "flag", "flag": "met_smith" }. (2) Reader: ContentPackLoader.Load(IContentSource) reads pack.json, then each listed file in index order. A JsonException becomes one problem for that file: file, line and column (LineNumber and BytePositionInLine are 0-based, so add 1), and the JSON path. Reading continues with the other files, so one run reports every file's problem. (3) Build and validation pass: merges sections across files in index order, recording each item's provenance (file plus JSON pointer). It checks pack-level rules: exactly one settings section; at most one synergy section; ids unique per section across the whole pack; file paths relative, forward slashes, no '..', ending in .json. It maps format records to the existing rules records (GameSettings, CharacterDefinition, ArchetypeDefinition, SynergySettings, EncounterDefinition with CombatantConfig) and calls GameContent.Create. GameContent.Create's RuleErrorDetail paths (for example characters/3/archetypeId) are translated through the provenance table into file locations (cast.json:/characters/0/archetypeId). Every problem comes back together in one refusal: Result<GameContent> failing with VALIDATION_ERROR, each Details entry's Path being '<file>:<json-pointer>' or '<file>:line L, column C' and its Message the problem. Content sources: IContentSource { Result<string> ReadText(string relativePath) }, with FolderContentSource (System.IO; for tests and the content check tool) and MemoryContentSource (tests) in the rules library; Godot implements GodotContentSource over Godot.FileAccess for res:// paths. GameContent gains Pack (PackInfo: Id, Name, StandIn), defaulting to an unnamed, not-stand-in pack for content built in C#. In Godot, GameHost reads the custom project setting ancient_order/content/pack (default res://content/standin) and loads through GodotContentSource. It exposes either Content plus Session, or ContentProblems (the list), and never throws on bad content. The stand-in content in godot/StandIn/StandInContent.cs moves into JSON under godot/content/standin/ and the C# file is deleted. The smoke run gets its content from the pack (through GameHost, or a GodotContentSource of its own) and takes its ids from a small constants class in godot/smoke.
tasks.interfaces: Produces: IContentSource (ReadText(relativePath) -> Result<string>), FolderContentSource(rootFolder), MemoryContentSource(map of path -> text), ContentPackLoader.Load(IContentSource) -> Result<GameContent>, and GameContent.Pack (PackInfo Id, Name, StandIn). Also the pattern T2-T9 extend: a new section or field = a format record + a mapping + validation with provenance, all in this loader. For Godot: GameHost.Content / GameHost.Session (null when content failed) and GameHost.ContentProblems (ImmutableArray<RuleErrorDetail>, empty on success), which screen flow (T13) shows instead of the start screen. For the content check tool (T11): Load over a FolderContentSource of any pack folder. Consumes: GameContent.Create and the existing rules records.

tasks.producer_notes: Follow ADR-064: ordered arrays wherever order matters, lookup-only maps never iterated, no sorted dictionaries, culture-invariant strings, refusals as Result values. The rules library must stay dependency-free (AORULES001); System.Text.Json is part of the framework, so it is allowed. Never deserialize JSON straight into rules records; map from format records, as SaveMapper does. Check that JsonSerializerOptions in .NET 10 offers AllowDuplicateProperties; if the strict preset JsonSerializerOptions.Strict fits the source-generated context, it may be used as the base. Keep IsAotCompatible clean (source generation only, no reflection fallback). Problem paths must name the file the item came from, not its merged index. Stand-in JSON must reproduce StandInContent.cs exactly (settings, both companions, both archetypes and the full decision profile, the two synergy bonuses with best-only, the encounter and enemy reaction skills). A test should prove the loaded pack matches. Avoid comments in pack files, even though the parser tolerates them, and confirm the Godot editor opens the project with the .json files present and no errors. Existing tests keep building content in C# through TestContent; do not convert them. Exported builds will later need *.json in each export preset's non-resource filter (export sprint, not now). Settings keep today's lineupSize field here; T6 replaces it with lineup limits.

tasks.title: Conversations play from content
tasks.description: The game session plays any conversation described in a content pack, from start to finish. One format covers one-on-one talks and narrated scenes: a conversation has participants and steps; each step has lines (spoken by a character, the narrator, or the player) and choices, and a step with no choices offers Continue. A pack file may hold several conversations. Nothing about a particular conversation lives in code. This is the base the mechanics tasks (T3–T6) attach to.
acceptance_criteria: Any conversation in a content pack — one-on-one or narrated, with any number of speakers — can be started, stepped through, and finished through the game session with no code change per conversation
Each step reports who is speaking (a character, the narrator, or the player), what is said, and its choices; a step with no choices reports a single Continue

Starting a conversation while one is running, or taking an unknown or unavailable choice, is refused and leaves the game unchanged; every change produces a new game state and leaves earlier ones unaltered
While a conversation is running, the game state records which conversation it is and which step the player is on
A choice or Continue destination can lead to another step or start another conversation, and an empty or unmatched destination list ends the conversation
SessionSnapshot.Conversation shows the current step with speaker names, and SessionSnapshot.LastChoice carries the report of the choice that produced the snapshot and is null after any other change
Conversations with references to missing characters, steps, or conversations, or duplicate step or choice ids, are refused at content load with their file locations
tasks.technical_approach: The conversation player lives in the rules library under rules/AncientOrder.Rules/Conversations/, with our own format (designer decision 2026-10-29 over Ink or Yarn Spinner). Content format (added to ContentFile as a conversations section; one file may hold many): conversation { id, title?, participants: [characterId], start?: [ { step, when? } ], steps: [ step ] }. Step: { id, lines: [ { speaker, text, when? } ], choices?: [ choice ], next?: [ destination ] }. Choice: { id, text, requires?, when?, lockedText?, effects?: [effect], reactions?: [override], next?: [destination] }. Destination: exactly one of { step } or { conversation }, plus an optional when. speaker is "narrator", "player", or a character id; those two ids are reserved and refused as character ids. Choice ids are unique within their conversation (not just the step), so conversation/choice names one choice. Rules records mirror this as immutable records: ConversationDefinition, StepDefinition, LineDefinition, ChoiceDefinition, Destination (ToStep | ToConversation), Speaker (Narrator | Player | Character(id)), plus ConversationCatalog (content order plus lookup) on GameContent.Conversations. GameState gains Conversation: ActiveConversation(ConversationId, StepId)? Pure functions in ConversationRules: Start(content, game, id), Choose(content, game, choiceId), Continue(content, game). Each returns Result<ConversationStep> carrying the new GameState and a ChoiceReport. Start resolves the opening step: the first start entry whose condition holds, or else the first step. Choose and Continue apply the choice's effects in written order, then reactions (T4), then record the choice (T5), then resolve next: the first destination whose condition holds. A step destination moves the conversation; a conversation destination ends this one and starts that one at its opening step; no destination ends the conversation (Conversation = null). A step whose choices are all hidden at run time offers Continue and follows the step's own next, so play can never stall. A choice applies completely or not at all; any refusal leaves the game unchanged. Session: GameSession.StartConversation(id), Choose(choiceId), and Continue() (new partial file GameSession.Conversations.cs; operations in ConversationOperations). Refusals use new ErrorCodes: CONVERSATION_NOT_FOUND, CONVERSATION_ALREADY_ACTIVE, NO_ACTIVE_CONVERSATION, CHOICE_UNAVAILABLE. Starting is also refused during combat. SessionSnapshot gains Conversation (ConversationView?) and LastChoice (ChoiceReport?), both derived on commit, as Synergy is. ConversationView: Id, Title, Participants (id, name), StepId, Lines (speaker kind, speaker id, speaker display name, text; hidden lines left out), Choices (id, text, Available, Requirement, LockedText; hidden choices left out), IsContinue. The player speaker shows the player's name and the narrator shows no name. LastChoice is the report of the choice that produced this snapshot and is null on every other commit. ChoiceReport: ConversationId, ChoiceId (null for Continue), Ended, NextConversationId, plus the lists T3 to T6 fill (TraitChanges, Reactions, RelationshipChanges, Joined, Left, FlagsSet, FlagsCleared). This task adds the effect pipeline as a union of effect records with its first effect, relationship { character, affection?, trust? }, applied through CharacterRules.ChangeRelationship and reported in RelationshipChanges. The loader validates references inside conversations: participants and speakers exist, step ids are unique per conversation, destinations and starts name real steps or conversations, and choice ids are unique per conversation.
tasks.interfaces: Consumes: the T1 loader (adds the conversations section and its format records), CharacterRules (names, relationship changes), GameContent. Produces: ConversationCatalog on GameContent; GameState.Conversation; ConversationRules.Start/Choose/Continue; session operations StartConversation(string id) -> Result<ConversationView>, Choose(string choiceId) -> Result<ChoiceReport>, Continue() -> Result<ChoiceReport>; SessionSnapshot.Conversation and SessionSnapshot.LastChoice; the Effect union and the ChoiceReport that T3, T4, T5, T6, and T9 extend; the hook points where T5 conditions apply (line when, choice when and requires, destination when, start when). tasks.title: Personality shifts and gates
tasks.description: A choice can shift the player's personality, and a choice can require a personality trait threshold before it can be taken. Each step reports a locked choice's in-world line for players and its requirement for the dev tools, and taking a choice reports what it shifted (shown to players only through their readout, ADR-075). The guarantee that every step has an ungated fallback is enforced by the content check (T11).
acceptance_criteria: A choice can shift any of the six traits; after every shift each trait stays within 5–35% and all six sum to 100%
A choice can require a personality trait threshold; such a choice is locked until it holds, and the step reports it as locked with its in-world line
Taking a choice reports the personality change it actually caused
A locked choice reports an in-world line to show (its own lockedText or the pack's default), and, for the dev tools, its requirement with the threshold and the player's current value
tasks.technical_approach: Adds the shift effect and personality reporting to the T2 pipeline, and makes trait gates show what they need. Effect format: { "type": "shift", "patience"?, "empathy"?, "cunning"?, "logic"?, "kindness"?, "charisma"? }, each an optional number (typed properties, so a misspelled trait is refused). It maps to PersonalityAdjustment and is applied through PersonalityRules.Adjust, which keeps every trait within 5–35% and the sum at 100. Several shift effects in one choice apply in written order. ChoiceReport.TraitChanges lists, in trait order (Patience to Charisma), each trait whose value actually changed, with before, after, and change: the personality that actually resulted, compared with the one before the choice. ChoiceReport also carries the choice's written shift totals (WrittenShift), which T4 reactions use (decision A). Gates use T5's trait condition { type: trait, trait, atLeast?, atMost? } in a choice's requires. The step's ChoiceView.Requirement for a trait gate is a TraitRequirement carrying trait, atLeast, atMost, the player's current value, and Met, so the dev tools (T37) can show, for example, 'Empathy 25%+ (you: 22%)'. Players never see requirement numbers (designer direction 2026-10-30). ChoiceView.LockedText is resolved by the rules: the choice's lockedText or, when it has none, the pack's default locked line (settings conversations.lockedText), so the panel always has an in-world line to show. TraitChanges and WrittenShift stay in the report for the dev tools; the conversation panel shows no shift numbers, and the party readout shows the resulting values. The always-available fallback rule is enforced by the content check (T11).

Produces: ShiftEffect (format and rules), ChoiceReport.TraitChanges (actual) and ChoiceReport.WrittenShift (authored totals per trait, for T4), and TraitRequirement detail (with the current value) in the requirement view read by the conversation panel (T17).

tasks.title: Archetype-driven reactions
tasks.description: When a choice shifts the player's personality, the characters present react according to their archetype's trait leanings (the designer's option C), with matching affection and trust changes. A choice can override a specific character's reaction — replacing it with written text and values, or silencing it. Archetype leanings are content added to the existing archetype records; the archetypes themselves are creative content, and stand-in archetypes are clearly marked stand-ins.
acceptance_criteria: A choice that shifts personality draws reactions from the characters present according to their archetype's leanings, so characters of different archetypes can react differently to the same choice; each reaction is reported with who reacted
A reaction changes the reacting character's affection and trust, within their allowed ranges
A choice can replace a specific character's reaction with written text and values, or silence it
Archetype leanings live in content; adding or changing an archetype needs no code change, and archetypes never change during play
Reactions follow the choice's written shift, so a choice still draws reactions when the player's trait is already at 35%

Each reaction reports a direction (warmer, cooler, or neutral for a written line with no change) and a strength (slight, clear, strong) with a written line chosen for that strength, so a screen can show it without numbers
Each character reports a demeanor toward the player (warm, neutral, wary, cold) worked out from their relationship, with the cutoffs in content
tasks.technical_approach: Archetype records gain optional reactions (content, added to the archetype format): { leanings: { patience?, empathy?, cunning?, logic?, kindness?, charisma? } (weights), minimum (the smallest score that draws a reaction), affectionPerPoint, trustPerPoint, approve, disapprove }, where approve and disapprove are each { clear, slight?, strong? } body-language lines (slight and strong fall back to clear). Text may use {name}, which is replaced with the reacting character's name. Rules: ReactionRules.React(content, game, conversation, choice, writtenShift). When a choice has a written shift (designer decision A: what the choice expresses, not how the personality actually moved), each participant who is a catalog character (in participant order) is scored. The score is the sum, over traits in trait order, of leaning times written shift. If its absolute value is below minimum, or the archetype has no reactions, there is no reaction. Otherwise the affection change is JsMath.Round(score × affectionPerPoint) and the trust change JsMath.Round(score × trustPerPoint); if both round to 0 there is no reaction. Approve is used when the score is positive, disapprove when negative. The change goes through CharacterRules.ChangeRelationship (clamped to −100..100), and the report gives the change actually applied. Choice overrides (reactions on the choice): { character, silence: true } removes that character's reaction; { character, text, affection?, trust? } replaces it with written text and values. An override fires whether or not the choice shifts personality. An override must name a participant (loader check). Tells (designer direction 2026-10-30: players see body language, not numbers): every reaction carries a Direction and a Strength. Direction is Warmer when the intended affection plus trust change is positive, Cooler when negative, and Neutral when zero (only a written override with no values). Strength comes from the larger of the intended affection and trust changes, before clamping, against settings tells { clearAt, strongAt } (defaults 3 and 8): below clearAt is Slight, at or above strongAt is Strong, otherwise Clear; a Neutral tell is Slight. Intended values are used so a character already at 100 still visibly approves, and archetype reactions and written overrides share one scale. An archetype reaction's text is the approve or disapprove line for its strength; a written override uses its own text. ChoiceReport.Reactions lists each reaction: character id, name, kind (Approve, Disapprove, Written), direction, strength, text, intended affection and trust, and the affection and trust change actually applied. Demeanor: DemeanorRules.Of(settings, relationship) gives each character's demeanor toward the player from affection plus trust against settings demeanor { warmAt, waryAt, coldAt } (defaults 50, -20, -60; the loader requires coldAt < waryAt < warmAt): Warm at or above warmAt, Cold at or below coldAt, Wary at or below waryAt, otherwise Neutral. ConversationView participants carry their Demeanor, and TownView people carry it (T7), so the screens can show posture before and during a conversation without numbers. Archetypes never change during play: they are read-only content (ADR-065).

tasks.technical_approach: The town in the rules library under rules/AncientOrder.Rules/Town/. Walkability split (designer decision A, 2026-10-29): the rules hold the authoritative position and answer whether a point is walkable; Godot finds paths and moves the player (T14), reporting positions the session checks. Coordinates: meters on the ground plane as [x, z] pairs; Godot maps them to Vector3(x, 0, z), Y up. Content format (towns section): town { id, name, ground: [polygon] (walkable areas, union), obstacles: [ { id, footprint: polygon, height, label? } ] (fixed this sprint), start: [x, z], reach?: number, people: [person], spots: [spot] }; polygon = [[x, z], ...] with at least 3 points. Person: { character, placements: [ { at: [x, z], facing?: degrees (0 faces -Z, clockwise seen from above), when? } ], opens (T8) }. A person is present when some placement's when holds; the first one that holds gives where they stand. Spot: { id, name?, area: exactly one of { circle: { center: [x, z], radius } } or { polygon }, trigger: interact | walkOver, shown?: bool (default true for interact, false for walkOver), when?, opens (T8) }. Settings gain startingTown (town id, optional so tests can run without towns) and reach (default 2.0). Rules records: Point(X, Z), Polygon, Area (Circle | PolygonArea), TownDefinition, ObstacleDefinition, PersonPlacement, SpotDefinition, TownCatalog on GameContent.Towns. Geometry (pure, exact): point in polygon by crossing number with points on an edge counted inside; point in circle and reach by squared distance; distance to a polygon area by squared point-to-segment distance. No square roots or other banned math (ADR-064). IWalkableGround { bool IsWalkable(Point) } with AuthoredGround: inside some ground polygon and inside no obstacle footprint. TownRules.Ground(content, townId) returns it. A real level's navigation data can implement the same interface later. GameState gains Town: TownPresence(TownId, Point Position)?. NewGame places the player at the starting town's start when startingTown is set. TownRules.Present(content, game) lists people present (with placement) and spots present, in content order. Re-derived on demand and never stored. Session: MovePlayer(double x, double z) -> Result<TownEvent> (T8 adds walk-over firing to it). Refused when there is no town or the town is complete (TOWN_NOT_ACTIVE), during a conversation or combat, for non-finite values (VALIDATION_ERROR), and off walkable ground (NOT_WALKABLE). SessionSnapshot gains Town (TownView?), derived on commit: id, name, ground polygons, obstacles (id, footprint, height, label), player position, reach, people present (character id, name, position, facing, CanOpen), spots present (id, name, area, trigger, shown, CanOpen); T8 fills CanOpen. The loader checks town references (startingTown, characters, spot ids unique per town) and shape (polygons of 3+ points, positive radius and height, finite numbers). Whether people, spots, and starts sit on walkable ground is the content check's job (T11). TownView people also carry Demeanor (T4's DemeanorRules), so the town can show posture without numbers (designer direction 2026-10-30). TownView also offers read-only helpers that wrap the rules' Geometry, so Godot never calls rules functions directly (ADR-057): IsInside(spotId, x, z) for a spot's area, InReach(characterId or spotId, x, z) using the settings reach and the same squared-distance rule the triggers use, and Reach.

tasks.description: Saving and loading keep everything this sprint adds: the town and the player's position, a conversation in progress, flags, remembered choices, conversations seen, the party and lineup, relationship changes, and the hand-off. tasks.technical_approach: Extends the existing save format in rules/AncientOrder.Rules/Saves/ (ADR-068) to version 2. SaveConstants.CurrentVersion = 2. SavedGame adds: party: [ids] (join order); town: { town, x, z }?; conversation: { conversation, step }?; memory: { flags: [..], chosen: [ { conversation, choice } ], seen: [..] }, each sorted ordinal (chosen by conversation, then choice) so the same game always writes the same bytes; handOff: { fight, lineup: [ids], town }?. The envelope adds summary: { townName?, situation: town | conversation | handOff | none }, written at save time from the content and the game, and SaveMetadata gains TownName and Situation so the slot list (T18, T20) can show them without current content. The rules records are still never serialized directly: SaveMapper maps both ways. SaveChecks checks the new fields: ids 1 to 64 characters, finite coordinates, no duplicates in party or memory arrays, a known situation. The upgrade step from version 1 (SaveUpgrades.Steps) works on the JSON object: party = a copy of lineup; memory = empty arrays; town, conversation, and handOff = null; summary = { situation: none }. SaveReconciler keeps today's character rules (fixed traits from content, missing characters dropped, new ones at their starting relationships) and adds, in this order, each listed in the LoadReport: party members not in content are dropped (PartyMemberDropped). Lineup members not in content, not in the party, or without combat stats are removed one by one (LineupMemberDropped); a lineup over the size limit is cleared (LineupCleared). Town: a missing town, or no town when content has a startingTown, puts the player at the starting town's start (TownReset); a position the town's IWalkableGround refuses moves the player to that town's start (PositionReset). Conversation: a missing conversation is ended (ConversationEnded); a missing step restarts the conversation at its opening step (ConversationRestarted), and effects already applied stay applied (designer decision A, 2026-10-29). Story memory is kept whole, even ids the content no longer uses. Hand-off: a missing fight, or a recorded lineup that is no longer ready for it, clears the hand-off and returns the player to the town (HandOffCleared). Reconcile never refuses. Session loads then publish a snapshot whose Conversation and Town views come from the reconciled state, so a mid-conversation save reopens at its step.

tasks.description: One check over a whole content pack that catches mistakes before they reach play: dead ends (a step with no choice that is always available), references to characters, archetypes, conversations, steps, towns, spots, or fights that don't exist, personalities outside 5–35% or not summing to 100%, malformed conditions and effects, and people, spots, or starting points off the walkable ground. tasks.technical_approach: The content check in rules/AncientOrder.Rules/Content/Check/. ContentCheck.Run(IContentSource) -> ContentCheckReport(GameContent? Content, ImmutableArray<RuleErrorDetail> Problems, ImmutableArray<RuleErrorDetail> Warnings). It runs the T1 loader, whose own checks cover format, broken references, personalities outside 5–35% or not summing to 100, and malformed conditions and effects. When the loader succeeds, it runs whole-pack analyses using the loader's provenance (ContentPackLoader gains an overload that also returns ContentProvenance), so every finding names its file and JSON location. Problems (fail): (1) dead ends: a step with choices where no choice is unconditioned (no requires, no when); hand-off choices do not count, because they are implicitly gated. Reported with the conversation and step. (2) Off the ground: a town's start, a person placement's point, or a spot's anchor that the town's AuthoredGround says is not walkable. The anchor is a circle's center, or for a polygon any vertex or the vertex average. (3) A condition reading a flag that no setFlag effect anywhere in the pack sets (typo catch). Warnings (printed, never fail): steps unreachable from their conversation's openings and destinations; conversations no opens entry or destination ever starts; flags set but never read. Console tool: tools/AncientOrder.ContentCheck (net10.0 exe, references the rules library, added to AncientOrder.sln so format and build cover it). Usage: dotnet run --project tools/AncientOrder.ContentCheck -- [pack folders...]. With no arguments it checks every godot/content/*/ folder containing pack.json, found relative to the repo root. Output: one line per finding, 'PROBLEM file:location: message' or 'WARNING file:location: message', then a summary per pack. Exit code 1 if any pack has problems, else 0. verify.ps1 gains a step after Test: 'Content check' running the tool with --no-build, failing verify on a non-zero exit and naming each problem. GameHost (T1) calls ContentCheck.Run instead of the bare loader. Any problem refuses play (ContentProblems shown by screen flow); warnings go to the Godot output with GD.Print. Further problems (design group 7, 2026-10-30, because players no longer see numbers): (4) a choice with requires and no lockedText when the pack sets no default locked line (settings conversations.lockedText), since the panel would have nothing to show; (5) empty or whitespace-only text a player would see (lines, choices, locked lines, reaction lines, feel lines). Further warning: a synergy bonus with no feel line while display.synergyNumbers is false, since players would not notice it. The tool keeps its logic in ContentCheckCli.Run(args, output, repoRoot), which returns the exit code; Program.Main only calls it, so tests (T35) need no process spawning. Further warning: conversation text (lines, choices, locked lines, reaction lines) containing a digit, since players should not see numbers in conversations (ADR-075).

tasks.description: The code that moves the player between screens and keeps them matched to the game session: the start screen leads into a new game or a loaded save; a menu opens over the town for the personality, party, and lineup view and the save and load screen; the hand-off swaps the town for the placeholder screen. tasks.technical_approach: main.tscn's root becomes ScreenFlow (godot/ui/ScreenFlow.cs). ScreenFlow gets Content, Session, and ContentProblems from GameHost (T1) and is the only node that holds the GameSession. Screens and presenters receive the session from it. The tree has: TownStage (T14, the 3D layer); a ScreenLayer CanvasLayer for the start, hand-off, and content-error screens; an OverlayLayer for the conversation panel, the game menu, the party screen, and the save screen; and a TopLayer for the error banner and the stand-in marker. Startup: when GameHost reports content problems, ScreenFlow shows ContentErrorScreen. In a release build that screen says only that the game's content failed to load, with Quit; in debug builds the dev tools (T37) add the full list. Otherwise it shows the start screen. Rendering: ScreenFlow subscribes with session.Subscribe(listener). The listener marshals every snapshot to the main thread (CallDeferred) before touching nodes, because an async load may commit off the main thread. Render(snapshot) chooses the base screen: Start while the local atStart flag is set (at launch and after Return to Start); otherwise HandOff when snapshot.HandOff is not null; otherwise Town when snapshot.Town is not null. It calls TownStage.Apply(snapshot.Town) whenever a town is present, and shows the conversation panel exactly while snapshot.Conversation is not null. New Game calls session.NewGame() and clears atStart. A load clears atStart once it succeeds. Menu: the ui_menu action (Esc) toggles GameMenu (Resume, Party, Save and Load) in the town, during a conversation, and at the hand-off. Opening it calls TownStage.Pause() and disables the panel's input; closing it resumes. Esc first closes an open party or save screen and then the menu. Refusals: every session call's failed Result goes to the ErrorBanner. Stand-in: when Content.Pack.StandIn is true, a 'STAND-IN CONTENT' marker sits in a corner of the TopLayer at all times. Project settings: display/window/stretch/mode = canvas_items, aspect = expand, base size 1280x720; screens anchor to the window edges so expand reveals space rather than letterboxing. Input actions: ui_menu (Esc), choice_1 to choice_9 (number keys and keypad), and dev_overlay (F3, read only by the dev tools). Dev tools seam (T37): ScreenFlow raises read-only C# events, SnapshotRendered(SessionSnapshot), LoadCompleted(LoadReport), and ContentChecked(ContentCheckReport). It makes one guarded call, DevTools.Install(this), inside #if AO_DEVTOOLS and only when OS.IsDebugBuild(). Test seam (T25): an exported AutoStart (default true) makes _Ready take content and the session from GameHost; tests set it to false and call Start(content, session, report) with their own in-memory content and saves.

tasks.technical_approach: A town scene in godot/town/ that is built entirely from SessionSnapshot.Town at run time, with no hand-made scene per town. TownStage.tscn (Node3D) holds: Ground (MeshInstance3D plus a StaticBody3D for picking), Obstacles, People, and Spots containers, Player (avatar), NavigationRegion3D, and TownCamera; T15 adds lighting and environment. TownStage.cs: Init(GameSession session, Action<RuleError> showError); Apply(TownView view). When the town id changes, Apply rebuilds everything: meshes via T15's builders, the navigation mesh, people, spots, and the player placed at the view's position. Otherwise it diffs people by character id (add, remove, or glide to a new position) and spots by id (add, remove, marker on or off). When the view's player position differs from the last position the stage reported (a load or new game), the avatar is placed there. Navigation (TownNavigation.cs wrapper, since Godot marks the navigation server API experimental): a NavigationMeshSourceGeometryData3D gets the ground triangles (AddFaces) and each obstacle footprint as a projected obstruction (AddProjectedObstruction with its height, carving). NavigationServer3D.BakeFromSourceGeometryData fills a NavigationMesh (agent radius about 0.4 m, matching the map's cell size), which is assigned to the region. Before the first path query, wait until NavigationServer3D.MapGetIterationId(map) has advanced past its value at assignment (poll in physics process, or use the map_changed signal); clicks are ignored until then. Do not use MapForceUpdate (deprecated in 4.7). Paths: NavigationServer3D.MapGetPath(map, from, to, optimize: true), with the target projected by MapGetClosestPoint. The avatar is moved along the points at an exported walk speed (default 4.5 m/s) by a Tick(double delta) method that _PhysicsProcess calls, so tests can drive time. Clicks: _UnhandledInput takes left clicks only after GUI has had them. It ray-casts from the camera (ProjectRayOrigin/ProjectRayNormal, PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D.IntersectRay with PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D) against named collision layers (PickLayers: ground, people, spots) and calls one of three public methods, which tests also call directly. WalkTo(Vector3 point). WalkToPerson(string characterId): path toward the person, arriving when TownView.InReach holds at 0.8 × reach; then session.MovePlayer, then session.TriggerPerson. WalkToSpot(string spotId): the same for interact spots using the area distance; then session.TriggerSpot. Reporting contract (T8): MovePlayer(x, z) is called on arrival at a ground destination; on entering or leaving any present walk-over spot's area (checked each tick with TownView.IsInside on the avatar's x, z); and before any trigger. If a report returns a TownEvent other than Nothing, walking stops. If a report is refused, the avatar snaps back to the last accepted position and the refusal goes to showError. Pausing: walking stops when Apply sees a conversation in the snapshot (SessionSnapshot.Conversation != null) or when screen flow calls Pause() for the menu (which reports the current position first only while the town is active, as described below). The destination is cleared, so after a conversation or the menu the player stands where they stopped and clicks again to move. Camera (designer decision A, 2026-10-29): TownCamera.cs, a fixed angle with zoom only. Perspective Camera3D at a fixed yaw (default 45 degrees) and high pitch (default about 55 degrees), smoothly following the player. The mouse wheel (input actions camera_zoom_in and camera_zoom_out) changes the distance between exported limits. Yaw, pitch, FOV, and limits are exported properties, tunable in the editor. Tells and demeanor (design group 7, 2026-10-30): Apply passes each person's Demeanor to their marker, and the stage tells markers where the player stands whenever it reports a position, so posture can face toward or away from the player. PlayTell(characterId, TellDirection, TellStrength) plays a reaction on that person's marker; the conversation presenter (T16) calls it. Geometry: walk-over tracking uses TownView.IsInside and arrival uses TownView.InReach (T7) rather than calling the rules' Geometry directly; arrival for a person uses 0.8 x reach through the same helper. Pause(): reports the current position first only while a town is active with no conversation in progress and no hand-off recorded, since the session refuses moves then (T7, T9); otherwise it just stops walking.
tasks.interfaces: Consumes: SessionSnapshot.Town (TownView) and SessionSnapshot.Conversation (T7, T2); session MovePlayer, TriggerPerson, TriggerSpot (T7, T8) and their TownEvent results; TownView.IsInside and InReach (T7) for walk-over tracking and arrival, so the stage uses only the session and its views (ADR-057) and agrees with the rules, which re-check every report. Produces for screen flow (T13): TownStage.Init(session, showError), Apply(TownView), Pause(), Resume(). For tests (T26, T27): WalkTo, WalkToPerson, WalkToSpot, Tick(delta), IsWalking, PlayerPosition, IsNavigationReady. For T15: the containers and build hooks its meshes and markers plug into. Also produces PlayTell(characterId, direction, strength) for the conversation presenter (T16); consumes Demeanor on TownView people (T7, T4).

tasks.technical_approach: The town's placeholder look, in godot/town/visuals/. PlaceholderMeshes.cs: ground meshes from the content polygons (Geometry2D.TriangulatePolygon on the x, z points, built with SurfaceTool into an ArrayMesh at y = 0, plus a matching ConcavePolygonShape3D for picking). Obstacle blocks extruded from each footprint to its height (walls plus a top cap via SurfaceTool), with an optional Label3D showing the obstacle's label. PersonMarker.tscn/.cs: a capsule body, a pick shape on the people layer, a Label3D name tag (billboard, fixed size, outlined, alpha cut disabled for clean text), and an interaction marker shown when CanOpen is true and highlighted when the player is within reach. SpotMarker.tscn/.cs: a flat, semi-transparent disc or polygon slightly above the ground, drawn only when the spot is shown, with a pick shape on the spots layer for interact spots and the same interaction marker. PlayerAvatar.tscn: a capsule in a distinct color with a small facing indicator. Materials: simple flat-colored StandardMaterial3D resources in godot/town/visuals/materials/, using the Equinox palette (leather browns for ground, metal grays for buildings, parchment for labels). Clearly placeholder: no textures, no models. Lighting: a DirectionalLight3D with shadows and a WorldEnvironment (ambient light, plain background color from the Equinox deep brown) added to TownStage.tscn. The 3D view fills the window at any size; UI scaling is set project-wide in T13. Body language on the capsules (designer decision 1A, 2026-10-30, until real animation exists): PersonMarker.SetDemeanor sets a resting posture relative to the player: Warm turns toward the player and leans slightly in, Neutral stands upright, Wary turns partly away, Cold turns away and hunches (a small forward tilt and lowered height). PersonMarker.PlayTell(direction, strength) briefly leans toward the player for Warmer or pulls back for Cooler, with the size and duration scaled by strength (Slight barely, Strong clearly), then settles back into the demeanor posture, using a Tween.
tasks.interfaces: Consumes: TownView data (ground and footprints, people with names and CanOpen, spots with area, trigger, shown, CanOpen) through TownStage's build hooks (T14); PickLayers; the Equinox palette values (T12's colors, copied into the 3D materials, since themes apply to UI only). Also produces PersonMarker.SetDemeanor(demeanor, playerPosition) and PlayTell(direction, strength). PersonMarker also exposes read-only Demeanor and LastTell (direction, strength) for the screen tests (T30).

tasks.technical_approach: ConversationPresenter (godot/ui/conversation/ConversationPresenter.cs) binds the ConversationPanel (T17) to the session. ScreenFlow gives it each rendered snapshot. When snapshot.Conversation appears, the panel opens at its current step. That covers a conversation started in the town and a mid-conversation save that was loaded; after a load LastChoice is null, so no outcome shows. When snapshot.LastChoice is set (the choice or Continue that produced this snapshot), the presenter builds an Outcome and hands it to the panel before the new step. The Outcome holds: the chosen choice's text as the player's line (none for Continue); each reaction in report order as its body-language line (the report's text, with {name} already replaced by the rules); and plain notices for party changes ('STAND-IN Smith joins the party.' style, built from Joined and Left names). The same notices are used for a hand-off. For each reaction whose character stands in the current town, it calls TownStage.PlayTell(characterId, direction, strength) so the capsule leans in or pulls back (designer decision 1A, 2026-10-30). Personality shifts are not shown in the conversation; the party readout (T19) shows the new values. When the choice ended the conversation (snapshot.Conversation is null) and the Outcome has anything to show, the panel stays open showing the Outcome with a single Close button. Close is presentation only, not a session call; afterwards the panel closes and the town resumes. Otherwise the panel closes at once. Choices and Continue go to session.Choose(choiceId) and session.Continue(); a refusal goes to the ErrorBanner and the panel stays on its step.

It stops mouse input so clicks do not reach the town. An optional header shows the conversation title when content gives one. The transcript area (a ScrollContainer over a VBox, scrolled to the bottom on change) shows two blocks. First, the Outcome of the previous choice (T16): the player's line under the player's name; each reaction's body-language line (TellLine variation); party notices (MutedLabel). Second, the current step's lines: a character's line under their name (TitleLabel-sized name, primary text), a narrator line without a name (NarrationLine), and a player line under the player's name. Below it sit the choices, a VBox of Buttons labelled '1. text', '2. text', and so on, in view order. A locked choice (Available false) is a disabled button with the LockedChoice variation. tasks.technical_approach: Two presenters connect the party and save screens to the session. PartyPresenter (godot/ui/party/PartyPresenter.cs) renders snapshot.Party (PartyView, T6) into the PartyScreen (T19) on every snapshot while it is open. A lineup toggle builds the new lineup from the current one: toggling on appends the member, and toggling off removes them. It calls session.SetLineup(ids); a refusal goes to the ErrorBanner, and the screen re-renders from the unchanged snapshot. SavePresenter (godot/ui/saves/SavePresenter.cs) wraps the session's async methods: ListSlots(), SaveToSlot(slot), LoadFromSlot(slot), and DeleteSlot(slot), which return ValueTask of Result. It calls them from the main thread and awaits them. It always hands the result back to the main thread explicitly (CallDeferred or Callable.From(...).CallDeferred()) before touching nodes; it does not rely on a main-thread SynchronizationContext. One operation runs at a time: the screen shows a busy state and disables its buttons until the result arrives. After a save or delete it refreshes the slot list. After a successful load it raises ScreenFlow.LoadCompleted(report) for the dev tools (T37) and closes the save screen and the menu, and the loaded snapshot renders. A refusal (for example, a damaged save) is shown inline on the save screen with the refusal's message. Release builds show no load adjustments: the reconciliation still happens; only the dev tools list it (designer decision 3A moved to the dev tools, 2026-10-30).

Produces: PartyScreen.Render(PartyView) and lineup toggles back to the session; SaveScreen.Render(slots, mode, busy) and its save, load, and delete requests; LoadCompleted(LoadReport) for the dev tools (T37).

tasks.technical_approach: Two parts: the Godot screen-test runner that every screen test uses, and the start-of-game tests. (1) Runner, an in-house replacement for GdUnit4Net and GoDotTest, which are VSTest-based and conflict with the solution's Microsoft.Testing.Platform runner (research 2026-10-29). Files live in godot/tests/. TestRunner.tscn and .cs: on _Ready it finds, by reflection, every public method marked [GodotTest] in classes under the AncientOrder.Tests namespace. It runs them one at a time in name order, each on a fresh instance with a fresh TestContext, and frees everything the test added. A test returns Task or void. TestContext provides: Root (a Node added to the tree for the test); NextFrame() and Frames(n), which await ProcessFrame; Press(action), which sends Input.ParseInputEvent for an InputEventAction press and release, then awaits a frame; StartGame(pack, saves?), which builds content through ContentCheck.Run over a MemoryContentSource and a GameSession with a MemorySaveBackend (or a given backend), instantiates main.tscn with ScreenFlow.AutoStart = false, and calls ScreenFlow.Start(content, session, report). Each test has a timeout (default 10 s) and fails with a message when it runs out. A minimal Assert class (Equal, True, NotNull, Contains, NoDigits) throws TestFailure. Output: 'PASS Class.Method' or 'FAIL Class.Method: message' per test, then a summary line. It exits through GetTree().Quit(1) on any failure, else Quit(0). An optional '--filter=text' user argument (OS.GetCmdlineUserArgs) runs matching tests only. Support: godot/tests/Support/TestPacks.cs builds small in-memory packs with JSON written in C#. Their text has no digits, so the no-numbers guards are meaningful. verify.ps1 gains a 'Godot screen tests' step after the smoke run: Invoke-Godot with --headless --path godot res://tests/TestRunner.tscn and a 300 s timeout. The Godot csproj removes tests/** from compilation in ExportRelease, as it does devtools/** (T37). (2) Start-of-game tests. tasks.technical_approach: All dev tools live in godot/devtools/ (namespace AncientOrder.DevTools). Inclusion: the Godot csproj defines its own symbol AO_DEVTOOLS for every configuration except ExportRelease, and removes devtools/** from compilation in ExportRelease (Compile Remove with the same condition). ScreenFlow's single call, DevTools.Install(this), sits inside #if AO_DEVTOOLS and also checks OS.IsDebugBuild() at run time. Our own symbol is used because a 2026-10-30 check found reports that DEBUG can stay defined in release exports. No scene or script outside devtools references anything inside it, and dev scenes are loaded only by devtools code, so the release build cannot pull them in. When export presets are created, their release preset excludes devtools/* (confirm the folder filter against a real export). DevTools.Install adds a CanvasLayer above the game and subscribes to ScreenFlow's read-only events (SnapshotRendered, LoadCompleted, ContentChecked). DevOverlay (DevOverlay.tscn and .cs): toggled by the dev_overlay action (F3). It is a right-side panel with compact, small, monospaced text and ignores the mouse except for its own scroll. It updates per snapshot, not per frame. Sections: Pack (id, stand-in); Player (exact traits); Last choice (written shift, actual trait changes before and after, and each reaction's character, kind, direction, strength, intended and applied affection and trust; relationship changes, flags set and cleared, joined and left, hand-off); People (each town person and conversation participant: affection, trust, demeanor); Conversation (id, step, each choice's availability, locked line, and requirement tree); Memory (flags, chosen and seen counts); Lineup (readiness and reason); Synergy (each SynergyResult: name, stat, step, value, match quality). RequirementText.cs formats RequirementView trees ('Empathy 25%+ (you: 22%) - unmet', with all, any, and not nesting). LoadReportNotice (tscn and cs): on LoadCompleted with any adjustments, a dismissible list of each adjustment's kind and detail (designer decision 3A, 2026-10-30, now dev-only). ContentProblemsList (tscn and cs): on ContentChecked with problems, replaces ContentErrorScreen's short message with every problem and warning as 'file:location: message'. Verify: verify.ps1 gains a 'Release build' step after Build, running dotnet build godot/AncientOrder.csproj -c ExportRelease, which proves the game compiles with the dev tools removed.
tasks.interfaces: Consumes: ScreenFlow events SnapshotRendered(SessionSnapshot), LoadCompleted(LoadReport), and ContentChecked(ContentCheckReport) (T13, T18, T11); the snapshot's ChoiceReport (T3, T4, T6), ConversationView requirements (T5), TownView people (T7), GameState memory and relationships, Synergy, and PartyView; theme trait colors (T12). Produces: the dev overlay, the load-adjustments notice, the content-problem list; the AO_DEVTOOLS symbol and the release-build exclusion; the verify step 'Release build'.
